result: Participants plan at least two future reaches simultaneously with an ongoing reach, as evidenced by significant reductions in inter-reach interval (IRI) from Horizon 1 to Horizon 2 across all dwell times (206-246 ms reduction, p<1e-10), with a further small improvement from H2 to H3 in the 75 ms dwell time condition (16 ms, p=5.30e-3).
evaluation: Claims C17-C22 provide strong statistical evidence with appropriate sample sizes (n=11), highly significant p-values, and consistent effects across multiple dwell time conditions. The inference that participants plan two targets ahead (C22) is reasonably supported by the H2 to H3 improvement, though the effect is small and only significant for the shortest dwell time.

result: Target jump experiments confirm that participants plan the +2 target simultaneously with executing the +0 reach and planning the +1 reach. When the +2 target was displaced, participants showed normal execution to the +1 target but significantly longer movement time to the +2 target (p=2.00e-4), with trajectories initially directed toward the pre-jump +2 position (minimum distance significantly lower, p=3.00e-4).
evaluation: Claims C23-C30 provide converging evidence from kinematic and temporal analyses. The experimental design appropriately tests the hypothesis, with proper controls (no-jump conditions) and multiple dependent measures. Statistical tests are appropriate with adequate sample size (n=10), though the manuscript should clarify whether multiple comparison corrections were applied across the multiple DVs.

result: Planning processes for multiple future movements interact and are not independent. When the +1 target was jumped, corrections were significantly slower and longer in H3 (where both +1 and +2 could be planned) compared to H2 (where only +1 could be planned), with longer movement time (p=1.80e-3) and trajectory length (p=3.00e-4), and trajectories closer to the +2 target (p=4.00e-3).
evaluation: Claims C31-C40 demonstrate interaction between planning processes through a well-designed comparison between H2 and H3 conditions. The logic is sound: if planning were independent, correction speed should be identical across horizons. The statistical evidence is strong (n=10, p<0.01 for all measures), and the interpretation of shared computational resources (C39) is reasonable though speculative.

result: Future reaches are not planned as a single 'motor chunk'. Evidence against chunking includes: (1) absence of pauses between reaches in speed profiles except H1 (Figure 1-supplement 1), (2) jumping the +2 target did not affect the +1 reach (p=0.56), and (3) jumping the +1 target allowed correction of the second segment without disturbing the first segment (p=1.64e-7 for shortened movement).
evaluation: Claims C41-C49 effectively rule out the chunking hypothesis through multiple lines of evidence. The logic is sound: chunked planning predicts pauses between chunks and obligatory replanning of entire chunks when any element is perturbed. The data clearly contradict these predictions. However, the characterization of what constitutes 'chunking' (C43) could be more precisely defined with citations.

result: Interaction between planning processes leads to biomechanically advantageous co-articulation of reach segments. When the +2 target demanded a rightward turn, the +1 reach curved left and vice versa. This effect was absent in H1 and H2 (slope not different from zero) but present in H3 for all dwell times (slope reliably <0), with continued growth from H3 to H4 for 75 ms dwell time (p=2.60e-3). Co-articulation was reduced with longer dwell times (F(2,20)=16.71, p=6.00e-4).
evaluation: Claims C50-C63 demonstrate co-articulation through sophisticated curvature analysis using PCA-based measures. The linear model controlling for previous target position (C54) is appropriate. The critical finding that co-articulation only occurs when planning processes temporally overlap (absent in H2, C56) strongly supports the interaction hypothesis. Statistical evidence is robust with appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons (C122).

result: Participants primarily fixate on the immediate next target (one saccade per reach in ~95% of trials) with information about subsequent targets processed parafoveally. Saccade angle was systematically shifted toward future target positions in H2 and H3 conditions (F(8,128)=12.60, p=3.12e-13), with no shift in H1 where future targets were not shown. Saccade timing relative to hand exit was consistent across horizons (F(2,36)=1.92, p=0.16).
evaluation: Claims C64-C72 provide novel insights into eye-hand coordination during sequential reaching. The eye-tracking data (n=19) are well-analyzed with appropriate preprocessing (C119). The inference about parafoveal processing (C65, C72) is reasonable given the one-saccade-per-reach pattern, though direct evidence of parafoveal processing would require additional experiments. The dissociation between eye movements (shifted in H2) and hand curvature (not shifted in H2) is intriguing (C94).

result: The abstract claims summarize the main findings: participants plan at least two future reaches simultaneously (C1), these planning processes interact (C2), corrections are slower with more future reaches planned (C3), curvature modifications occur only with temporal overlap of planning (C4), and these interactions may enable smooth sequential action production (C5).
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 accurately summarize the experimental findings detailed in the results section. C1-C4 are well-supported by the data. C5 is appropriately qualified as speculative ('may enable') and represents a reasonable interpretation of the functional significance of the findings, though it remains a hypothesis requiring further testing.

result: Comparison with prior finger sequence studies suggests that the planning horizon effect is more pronounced in finger sequences than reaching sequences. The authors speculate this may be due to differences in effector constraints (fingers can begin flexing in advance) or cue-to-action mapping complexity (direct spatial mapping vs. abstract number-to-finger mapping).
evaluation: Claims C73-C77 appropriately cite prior work (Ariani et al., 2021) but the comparison is qualitative rather than quantitative. The proposed explanations (C75, C76) are speculative and not directly tested. The conclusion (C77) is reasonable but would benefit from more systematic comparison of task parameters between studies. This represents useful discussion but not a primary empirical contribution.

result: The discussion relates findings to prior work on neural mechanisms, particularly Ames et al. (2019) showing orthogonal subspace replanning. The authors propose two possible mechanisms for the observed interaction: split neural resources or chunked replanning, and conclude that target perturbations demonstrate obligatory interaction between future movement plans.
evaluation: Claims C78-C82 appropriately contextualize findings within existing literature. The citation to Ames et al. (2019) is accurate (C78-C79). The proposed mechanisms (C80-C81) are speculative but reasonable. The conclusion about obligatory interaction (C82) is well-supported by the empirical data, though the specific mechanism remains uncertain.

result: The discussion proposes neural mechanisms for planning interactions, contrasting two hypotheses: (1) orthogonal planning with execution-planning interaction, or (2) direct interaction between preparation processes. The authors favor the latter based on absence of co-articulation in H2, but acknowledge that electrophysiology experiments are needed to determine the exact mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C83-C92 present thoughtful speculation about neural mechanisms, appropriately citing relevant literature (Zimnik & Churchland 2021, Fusi et al. 2016, Rigotti et al. 2013). The inference favoring direct interaction (C90) based on H2 data is reasonable but not definitive. The acknowledgment that further experiments are needed (C91) is appropriate. This represents valuable theoretical discussion but not empirical evidence.

result: The discussion proposes that information about future targets may be available first in eye movement circuitry and later in upper limb control areas, based on the observation that gaze shifts occur in H2 despite no hand curvature changes. The authors acknowledge this requires further investigation.
evaluation: Claims C93-C96 present an interesting speculation about differential timing of information availability across motor systems. The observation (C94) is valid, but the interpretation (C95) is highly speculative and alternative explanations are not considered. The acknowledgment that further studies are needed (C96) is appropriate. This represents a hypothesis for future work rather than a supported conclusion.

result: The methods describe the experimental design: 11 participants (later 10 for jump experiments) performed 14-reach sequences in a robotic exoskeleton with targets on a hexagonal grid (1 cm radius, 4 cm spacing). Dwell times were 75, 200, or 400 ms. Horizons 1-5 showed 1-5 future targets. A separate group of 19 participants completed eye-tracking experiments. All procedures were ethically approved.
evaluation: Claims C13-C113 provide detailed methodological information that appears complete and appropriate. Sample sizes are adequate for within-subject designs. The experimental manipulations (dwell time, horizon) are well-controlled. Participant characteristics are reported. Ethical approval is documented (C103). The methods support reproducibility of the experiments.

result: The analysis methods include: IRI defined as time between target entries; curvature analysis using PCA on spatially resampled trajectories, controlling for previous target position with linear models; exclusion of reaches near workspace boundaries to prevent predictability; appropriate statistical tests (repeated measures ANOVA) with Holm correction for multiple comparisons.
evaluation: Claims C114-C122 describe sophisticated and appropriate analysis methods. The IRI definition is clear (C114). The curvature analysis using PCA is innovative and well-justified (described in detail in text). The exclusion criteria (C115) appropriately control for potential confounds. Statistical methods (C121-C122) are appropriate with proper correction for multiple comparisons. The methods support the validity of the results.

result: The introduction establishes that sequential movements require proactive planning, cites extensive prior work showing benefits of future information across multiple motor domains, notes that planning and execution occur in overlapping brain areas, describes the orthogonal subspace hypothesis from Zimnik & Churchland (2021), and identifies the knowledge gap regarding planning of multiple future reaches and their interactions.
evaluation: Claims C6-C12 provide appropriate background and motivation. The citations appear accurate and comprehensive (C8 cites multiple domains). The description of the orthogonal subspace hypothesis (C11) correctly attributes it to Zimnik & Churchland 2021. The identification of the knowledge gap (C12) appropriately motivates the study. This represents standard introduction content that accurately represents prior work.
